entries.title: Lumpl and Goliath: The Statue and the Clay
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the full article and its matching dataset record. Checked the attribution and bibliographic date for Allan Gibbard’s Contingent Identity; the original Lumpl/Goliath setup, persistence criteria, shared actual history, and squeezing counterfactual; the logical framing of identity and modal difference; Gibbard’s account of proper names and modal predication; the families of responses and the existence of scholarly disagreement; the distinction between source-based history and editorial teaching analogies; and reconciliation of the revised Further Reading URLs and order with a proposed data patch. This status records traceability, not the truth of contingent identity, a settled solution, exhaustive literature review, or expert review.
entries.summary: The article has been corrected to match Gibbard’s original two-piece statue scenario: joining the halves begins the statue and clay piece together, and smashing the statue ends both. It now distinguishes the actual story from Gibbard’s counterfactual in which squeezing the clay into a ball leaves Lumpl existing while Goliath ceases, and identifies Gibbard’s persistence criteria as part of his proposal rather than settled ordinary usage. The article frames constitution, identity, revisionary/eliminativist, and contingent-identity approaches as competing families, states that the issue remains disputed, and labels person/body and ship/timber comparisons as teaching analogies. Relevant passages from the primary article, two SEP entries, and Wolfgang Schwarz’s scholarly survey were read; bibliographic metadata was separately verified. The revised article’s four Further Reading URLs and their order are reproduced exactly in the proposed data patch. This audit did not edit data/experiments.json; unrelated shared-worktree changes are outside this item review.

sources.title: Contingent Identity
sources.author: Allan Gibbard
sources.publication: Journal of Philosophical Logic, vol. 4, no. 2 (1975), pp. 187–221; full text consulted in a University of San Diego-hosted PDF reproduction.
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the full work; the article was not read cover to cover.
sources.exact_locations_read: §I and pp. 188–192, especially pp. 189–192: Gibbard’s stipulated persistence criteria for lumps and statues; the two-half statue of the infant Goliath, joined halves creating a statue and a new piece of clay together, and the smashing that ends both; his identity proposal and squeezing-into-a-ball counterfactual. Pp. 193–194 on the systematic physical account and the challenge to rigid-name semantics; pp. 210–211 on modal and counterfactual predication for concrete things and individual concepts.
sources.limitations: Primary evidence for what Gibbard proposes and argues, not evidence that his metaphysical conclusion succeeds. Gibbard says his persistence criteria need only fit ordinary usage roughly and could be stipulated for the argument. Only relevant passages, not the complete article, were read. The online copy is a hosted reproduction rather than the publisher platform.

sources.title: Material Constitution
sources.author: Ryan Wasserman
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 2009, substantive revision 2021; Spring 2024 archived version consulted.
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the archived full entry; the complete entry was not read cover to cover.
sources.exact_locations_read: Introduction and §1, “The Puzzles,” especially “The Puzzle of the Statue and the Clay” and the five-reply outline; §2, “Coincident Objects,” especially the constitution view, coinciding objects, and grounding objection. The read passages discuss why duplicates that share matter and many properties appear to differ in modal or persistence conditions, and outline eliminativist, dominant-kinds, relative-identity, and deflationist strategies.
sources.limitations: A scholarly survey, not a primary statement by every theorist it discusses and not an exhaustive map of the literature. Its David/Lump setup differs in details from Gibbard’s named Goliath/Lumpl story. The entry evaluates popular replies but does not establish a consensus or settle the dispute.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Gibbard’s example begins when a sculptor joins two halves of a clay statue of the infant Goliath, simultaneously bringing into existence a statue and a new piece of clay, and the sculptor’s later smashing ends both.
claim_evidence.source_title: Contingent Identity
claim_evidence.exact_location: §I, p. 191: the two-half statue story and the simultaneous beginning and ending; compare pp. 190–191 on persistence criteria.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text directly gives the two-piece setup, joins the halves to create the statue and piece of clay at once, and says that smashing the statue ends both after the same duration. The revised article now follows that setup rather than attributing a generic lump-shaped-into-a-statue and squashing-flat variant to Gibbard.
claim_evidence.limitation: This establishes Gibbard’s presented story, not that his stipulated identity conditions are the only correct ones.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the inaccurate simplified version with the two-piece creation and shared ending from Gibbard’s text.

claim_evidence.material_claim: On Gibbard’s persistence criteria, a lump can survive being reshaped into a ball while the statue ceases; he uses this as a counterfactual in which both exist but are nonidentical.
claim_evidence.source_title: Contingent Identity
claim_evidence.exact_location: §I, pp. 189–192, especially pp. 191–192: lump and statue criteria and the squeezing-into-a-ball counterfactual.
claim_evidence.finding: Gibbard explicitly says that under the criteria he has given, the statue would cease while Lumpl survives in a new shape, though both exist and are not identical in the counterfactual. He frames this as his argument for contingent identity.
claim_evidence.limitation: Gibbard calls his criteria approximate and allows that they may be stipulative; the counterfactual and his account of modal identity are disputed rather than a settled solution.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: tied the survival contrast expressly to Gibbard’s stipulated criteria and stated the counterfactual as nonidentity despite both existing.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Gibbard’s actual identity claim and the apparent modal contrast create a problem about strict identity, properties, and persistence rather than an uncontested demonstration of two objects.
claim_evidence.source_title: Contingent Identity; Identity
claim_evidence.exact_location: Gibbard, §I, pp. 191–192, on actual identity and contingent nonidentity; Noonan and Curtis, SEP Identity §7, on the example, the Kripkean denial-of-identity response, and the continuing controversy.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources support presenting Gibbard’s conclusion as an argument and a live metaphysical dispute. The revised article explicitly says that strict identity precludes literal property difference, then distinguishes Gibbard’s counterfactual claim from rival accounts.
claim_evidence.limitation: The sources do not settle whether contingent identity is coherent or whether Gibbard’s case is persuasive.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the prior unqualified ‘they seem to differ’ framing with an explicit statement of the inferential tension and its disputed status.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Constitution views, identity views, eliminativist or revisionary views, and contingent-identity proposals are competing approaches; the coincident-object approach faces a grounding question about differences in kind and persistence.
claim_evidence.source_title: Material Constitution; Contingent Identity
claim_evidence.exact_location: Wasserman, SEP Material Constitution, introduction and §1, ‘The Puzzle of the Statue and the Clay’ and its five replies; §2, ‘Coincident Objects,’ including the grounding objection at the discussion of shared parts and properties. Schwarz, §§2–4, on contingent identity and its objections/accounts.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP entry explicitly distinguishes constitution-is-identity, constitution-is-not-identity, and revisionary approaches, and surveys eliminativist, dominant-kinds, relative-identity, and deflationist replies. It calls coinciding objects a popular response and states the grounding challenge. Schwarz surveys reasons for and against contingent identity. The revised article presents its short list as broad families, not an exhaustive or agreed taxonomy.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s compressed teaching summary is not itself a full taxonomy of material-constitution theories; different views need not fit mutually exclusive labels.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: removed oversimplified claims that monism is merely redescribing one object and that all object-denial theories reduce straightforwardly to particles arranged statue-wise; qualified the categories and emphasized open disagreement.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Gibbard’s contingent-identity proposal depends on his treatment of persistence criteria, proper names, and modal predication; the proposal is not a settled account of ordinary object identity.
claim_evidence.source_title: Contingent Identity; Wolfgang Schwarz, ‘Contingent Identity’
claim_evidence.exact_location: Gibbard, §§I–II, pp. 190–194, and pp. 210–211; Schwarz, §§2 and 4, especially the discussion of Gibbard’s individual-concept semantics and the semantic contribution of singular terms to modal predication.
claim_evidence.finding: Gibbard develops persistence criteria, an account of proper names, and an account of modal/counterfactual properties as part of his defense. Schwarz explains the proposal in terms of individual concepts and modal predicates sensitive to more than reference. The revised article presents these as Gibbard’s commitments, not as consensus.
claim_evidence.limitation: This brief educational summary omits the formal details and objections to Gibbard’s semantics; a survey and selected primary passages cannot establish that his theory succeeds.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: identified the assumptions as part of Gibbard’s proposal and qualified the conclusion as disputed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The person/body and ship/timber comparisons are teaching analogies, not identical historical formulations attributed to Gibbard; ship replacement is a related but structurally different persistence question.
claim_evidence.source_title: Revised article framing; Identity; Material Constitution
claim_evidence.exact_location: Revised article §§5 and 7. For context, Noonan and Curtis, SEP Identity §7 (Lewis’s person/body case); Wasserman, SEP Material Constitution §1 (Ship of Theseus replacement story).
claim_evidence.finding: The article labels these comparisons as analogies, distinguishes the person/body question from Gibbard’s specific example, and notes that ship cases typically focus on changing parts. The source passages support the relevant context; the analogy and teaching choice are editorial framing.
claim_evidence.limitation: No claim is made that the cases are interchangeable or that Gibbard originated these extensions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly labeled the comparisons as teaching analogies and stated their structural differences.

entries.title: The Problem of the Many (Tibbles the Cat)
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and its matching local dataset record. Checked Unger’s 1980 attribution and cloud-boundary setup; Geach’s Tibbles/hairs passage, the argument yielding 1,001 cat-candidates, and Geach’s own relative-identity response; the article’s distinction between those formulations; the assumptions, claims, qualifications, and scholarly objections attached to the outlined responses (restricted composition/nihilism, overpopulation, relative identity, almost-identity, semantic vagueness and epistemicism, and vague parthood); the educational framing and ordinary-counting qualifications; the difference between vague-boundary/candidate-counting puzzles and the separate Tibbles-and-tail parthood/persistence story; bibliographic names, dates, edition and page details; and alignment of Further Reading URLs/order with the proposed data patch. Status records traceability, not that any philosophical argument succeeds, that one response is correct or consensus, exhaustive literature review, or expert review.
entries.summary: The revised article separates Unger’s original cloud-based many-or-none dilemma from Geach’s Tibbles argument. It now states that Geach’s example begins with at least 1,000 identifiable hairs, considers distinct feline-tissue masses omitting one hair at a time, and uses relative identity to say that different masses can be the same cat. It no longer describes this as a single generic taxonomy: the solutions and their objections are attributed as contested alternatives, including distinctions between Unger’s radical nihilist conclusion and restricted composition, between supervaluationism and indeterminate reference, and between Geach’s relative identity and Lewis’s almost-identity account. The cat-loses-its-tail example is explicitly separated as a parthood/persistence puzzle. Primary passages by Unger and Geach and relevant SEP sections were read; the article states that complete primary works were not read cover to cover. The local data patch uses the two stable archive URLs in the revised Further Reading order and leaves the read-only dataset unchanged.

sources.author: Peter Unger
sources.publication: Midwest Studies in Philosophy 5 (1980), 411–467; DOI 10.1111/j.1475-4975.1980.tb00416.x. Full text consulted via a PDF reproduction; the publisher’s PDC record was checked separately for bibliographic details.
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the full work; the full-text PDF was retrieved and parsed, but only the opening pages relevant to the cloud setup and argument were read for this audit.
sources.exact_locations_read: Printed pp. 411–415, especially the opening discussion of vagueness and clouds (§1) and the beginning of the formal cloud argument (§2): Unger introduces the named problem, describes gradually dispersed droplets, and states the many-or-none dilemma. The article’s claim about Unger extending the topic to other kinds was checked at p. 411, lines naming stones, tables, and hands.
sources.limitations: Only relevant passages were read, not the entire paper or all of its later argumentation. The primary text establishes Unger’s formulation and what he argues, not that its premises or conclusion are sound. The full text was read from a third-party PDF reproduction rather than the publisher-hosted paywalled copy.

sources.title: Reference and Generality: An Examination of Some Medieval and Modern Theories
sources.author: Peter Thomas Geach
sources.publication: Third edition, Cornell University Press, 1980, §110, “How is ‘is the same A as’ related to a proper name for an A?”; first edition 1962. Edition and publication details checked against the scanned title page and Google Books bibliographic record.
sources.access_level: Selected passage in a scanned full-book PDF; PDF pages 107–108 were parsed as text and the relevant §110 passage was read. The entire book was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §110, the passage beginning “The fat cat sat on the mat. There was just one cat on the mat.” It states the 1,000-hair assumption, considers masses of feline tissue each omitting one hair, derives the apparent 1,001-cat result, and then says the distinct masses are the same cat while the original story of one cat stands.
sources.limitations: The textual copy was obtained from an unofficial third-party scan; the official Google Books page confirms the third edition and publisher metadata but does not expose the argument passage. The scan’s PDF page numbers are not substituted for unverified printed pagination. The primary text establishes Geach’s proposal, not its correctness or acceptance.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Unger introduced the named Problem of the Many in 1980 and presented it through a cloud with gradually fading boundaries and multiple overlapping candidate aggregates, generating a many-or-none dilemma.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many; The Problem of the Many (publisher record); The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Unger, printed pp. 411–415, especially §§1–2; PDC publisher record, bibliographic metadata; Weatherson, SEP Winter 2023, §1.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary paper supports the attribution and the cloud-based candidate-aggregate setup. Unger frames the outcome as a dilemma if the described ordinary cloud exists and argues that there are many equally eligible overlapping candidates. The revised article presents this as Unger’s stipulated philosophical argument, not as an established empirical count or quote.
claim_evidence.limitation: The source establishes Unger’s argument, not the truth of its premises or conclusion; the full article was not read cover to cover.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: separated the cloud formulation from the cat example and marked it as a paraphrased stipulated dilemma rather than an empirical claim.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Geach’s Tibbles setup uses a cat with at least 1,000 identifiable hairs, considers tissue masses omitting one hair, derives an apparent 1,001-cat result, and responds that distinct tissue masses can be the same cat.
claim_evidence.source_title: Reference and Generality; The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Geach, Reference and Generality, 3rd ed. (1980), §110, PDF pages 107–108; Weatherson, SEP Winter 2023, §§1, 5, and 7.1.
claim_evidence.finding: Geach’s passage directly contains the hair/tissue construction, the apparent 1,001 result, and his resolution in terms of the different masses being the same cat. The revised article now distinguishes this relative-identity move from Unger’s cloud-based setup and marks the proposal as controversial.

claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the earlier generic atom/hair vignette with Geach’s actual omission-of-one-hair construction and explained his response.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Problem of the Many is about vague boundaries and competing candidate objects, but its relation to vagueness does not make it identical to the Sorites or to persistence-through-part-change puzzles.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (Unger); The Problem of the Many (SEP); Identity Over Time (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Unger, pp. 411–415; Weatherson, SEP §1 (vague predicates, cloud boundaries, and solution domains) and §9 (separate Tibbles-and-tail parthood example); Gallois and Kurtsal, SEP Spring 2026 §§1 and 4 (identity and persistence through changing parts).
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP survey explicitly distinguishes the problem’s apparent connection to vague predicates from deeper composition and identity issues, and its §9 tail story is a separate time-sensitive parthood puzzle. The identity-over-time source supports broad context only. The revised article says both puzzles are related but not the same, and directs the Tibbles-and-tail attribution to Weatherson §9.
claim_evidence.limitation: The identity-over-time source is a general secondary account and does not itself establish the Tibbles-tail example. The distinction is conceptual/editorial framing grounded in the SEP’s presentation.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified that Unger’s cloud case, Geach’s Tibbles masses, and the cat-loses-its-tail story are distinct presentations/questions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The outlined metaphysical responses include restricted composition or Unger-style nihilism, overpopulation, relative identity, and Lewis’s almost-identity proposal, with objections and different costs.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (SEP); Reference and Generality
claim_evidence.exact_location: Weatherson, SEP §§2–6; Geach, §110 for the cat/relative-identity proposal.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP surveys these as separate, competing options and gives objections; it notes overpopulation has defenders, distinguishes Unger’s radical conclusion from composition theories, and discusses challenges to both relative identity and almost-identity. The revised article now avoids collapsing all responses into “many cats” or a single almost-identity view.
claim_evidence.limitation: The selected responses are illustrative, not exhaustive. No claim is made that any response is settled or accepted by consensus.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced compressed, potentially conflating solution labels with a qualified list of distinct response families and acknowledged disagreement.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Semantic vagueness solutions, including supervaluationism and epistemicism, do not amount simply to saying every candidate is an equally permissible referent for the name Tibbles.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Weatherson, SEP §7, especially §§7.1–7.3 and its discussion of supervaluationist precisifications, penumbral connections, epistemicism, and semantic indeterminacy in names/demonstratives.
claim_evidence.finding: The source distinguishes supervaluationist treatment of vague predicate extensions from related indeterminacy about demonstratives/names and records objections to the supervaluationist package. The revised article says candidate classifications can vary across admissible precisifications while “there is one cloud” may remain true, and does not identify that with unrestricted reference-indeterminacy.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP entry itself notes outstanding objections and that the success of vagueness-based solutions is unsettled; the article gives a brief teaching summary rather than a full semantics.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: corrected the earlier overbroad description of supervaluationism as each candidate being a permissible referent and stated its contested status.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Some proposed responses locate indeterminacy in parthood/composition, while such moves remain controversial and do not automatically eliminate the many-candidates difficulty.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Weatherson, SEP §9, on van Inwagen’s vague parthood/fuzzy constitution account and the difficulties of selecting among candidate objects.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP describes a proposal to treat parthood as vague but questions how that handles the many candidate objects; it also distinguishes the cloud case from cats and people in the view discussed. The article avoids presenting ontological vagueness as a simple or accepted solution.
claim_evidence.limitation: The sources survey but do not settle whether ontological vagueness is coherent or whether it solves all versions of the problem.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: retained the metaphysical-vagueness option but made its contested and incomplete status explicit.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Lewis’s almost-identity response treats everyday counting as sometimes relying on almost-identity rather than strict identity; this is one proposal, not an established fact about ordinary counting.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Weatherson, SEP §6, including the statement that Lewis proposes counting by almost-identity and the section’s objections about strict identity and non-almost-identical candidates.
claim_evidence.finding: The source supports attributing the proposal to Lewis and describes objections. The revised article explicitly calls it one response and says other philosophers reject the analysis; it does not infer that ordinary counting in fact works this way.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a contested account of counting language and identity, not an empirical finding about speakers or a consensus view.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the counting claim as an attributed response and stated that its consequences depend on disputed assumptions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Unger extends the argument beyond clouds to other ordinary kinds, while the article’s crowd extension is editorial teaching framing.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (Unger); The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Unger, p. 411, lines naming stones, tables, and hands; Weatherson, SEP §§1–2 on objects including humans and the extension of the problem beyond clouds.
claim_evidence.finding: Unger explicitly says he will extend his arguments from clouds to other ordinary kinds, including stones, tables, and hands. The revised article attributes those examples to him and labels only the further crowd analogy as editorial framing.
claim_evidence.limitation: The crowd example is not represented as a historical example or as a separately sourced case.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: corrected the scope note so Unger’s own extensions are not mislabelled as editorial analogies.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The article’s ‘more detailed physical description does not by itself settle the count’ sentence is an interpretive explanation of the puzzle, not a claim that science can never contribute.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Problem of the Many (Unger); The Problem of the Many (SEP)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Unger, pp. 413–415 on gradual dispersion and equally eligible overlapping complexes; Weatherson, SEP §1 and §7 on the setup and candidate extension issue.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources frame the problem around multiple candidate aggregates and the absence of a uniquely favored one under the stipulated assumptions. The revised article limits its claim to physical description alone not settling which collections count as the object.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is an explanatory inference from the philosophical setup, not an independent result in physics or a universal claim that further empirical information is irrelevant.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: recast the statement as a limited interpretive point tied to the stipulated setup.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The revised Further Reading entries, their stable URLs and order match the proposed data patch; the target dataset record was not modified.
claim_evidence.source_title: Revised target article; matching local data record; proposed data patch
claim_evidence.exact_location: Article §9 and research/source-review-batch15-item-problem-of-the-many-data-patch.json; read-only data/experiments.json object with id problem-of-the-many.
claim_evidence.finding: The article lists the Weatherson Winter 2023 archive first and the Gallois–Kurtsal Spring 2026 archive second; the proposed patch contains those same URLs in that order and sets date_verified to 2026-11-01. The input dataset still has its prior date and was not edited.
claim_evidence.limitation: Local metadata reconciliation only; the patch is a proposed local file, not an applied dataset change.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: created the requested data patch only; did not modify data/experiments.json.

unresolved_limits: No named or qualified human subject-matter expert reviewed the article; no expert-review claim is made.
Only relevant passages, not the complete Unger article or Geach book, were read cover to cover; the primary Geach passage came from an unofficial scan.
The SEP survey is a selective secondary overview, not an exhaustive history of the literature; competing proposals and their criticisms are not settled by this audit.
The audit verifies attribution and traceability, not the truth or soundness of Unger’s or Geach’s arguments, or which theory of identity, vagueness, composition, or counting is correct.

entries.reviewer_type: AI-assisted claim-level source audit with self-check after edits; no human expert review is claimed.
entries.title: The Condorcet Paradox
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the article and matching dataset entry. Checked the historical attribution and 1785 publication framing against the original French passage and modern reference works; the stated three-voter profile and pairwise-majority calculations; the assumptions of strict transitive rankings and pairwise majority; the absence of a Condorcet winner; the distinction between a cycle and sequential agenda effects; Condorcet-consistent and scoring procedures; single-peaked domain restrictions; the relationship to Arrow's theorem; probability-model assumptions and scholarly disagreement about empirical prevalence; and editorial/normative teaching prompts. The status records source traceability, not the truth of every normative interpretation, exhaustive literature coverage, consensus, or expert review.
entries.summary: The revised article preserves the illustrative cycle while stating the profile and pairwise-majority assumptions explicitly. It separates the cycle in the pairwise relation from agenda effects in sequential voting, qualifies the discussion of scoring rules and domain restrictions, describes Arrow as a broader related result rather than a theorem derived from this example, and distinguishes conditional model-based likelihood from contested empirical prevalence. The original French essay's relevant discussion of a three-candidate election and majority judgments was accessed in OCR text; the article now identifies its example as a modern teaching presentation rather than a verbatim reconstruction of Condorcet's profile. Modern reference and scholarly sources were read at relevant passages. Dataset references were reconciled to the revised Further Reading list; the dataset itself was not modified.

sources.title: Essai sur l'application de l'analyse à la probabilité des décisions rendues à la pluralité des voix
sources.author: Nicolas de Condorcet
sources.publication: Paris: Imprimerie Royale, 1785; digitized edition hosted by the Internet Archive.
sources.access_level: Selected excerpt of the scanned work, accessed in the Archive.org DjVu OCR text; the complete work was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: Discours préliminaire, the passage beginning “Il nous reste à donner un dernier exemple: c'est le cas d'une élection entre trois candidats,” through the discussion of combinations of preference propositions and the contradictory conclusions arising from some combinations. No page number is asserted because the extracted OCR's printed Roman folio markers are unreliable in this passage.
sources.limitations: The source is in French and was consulted through machine OCR rather than a critical edition or facsimile page inspection. The passage supports Condorcet's discussion of three-candidate preference judgments and possible inconsistency; it is not identical to the article's modern three-voter profile in the exact displayed notation.

sources.title: Social Choice Theory
sources.author: Christian List
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 2013, substantive revision 14 October 2022; §§1.1, 3.1, and 3.3.1.
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the current entry were read through the page's extracted text; the entire entry was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §1.1 attributes pairwise majority voting and the Condorcet paradox to the 1785 Essay and gives a one-third/one-third/one-third cycle; §3.1 defines profiles and pairwise majority and discusses the dependence of cycle frequencies on assumptions; §3.3.1 explains single-peaked domains and Black's result that cycles cannot occur under that restriction.
sources.limitations: Secondary scholarly synthesis, not Condorcet's testimony. Probability statements are model-dependent; the entry itself notes that departures from impartial culture can substantially reduce cycle probabilities.

sources.title: Voting Methods
sources.author: Eric Pacuit
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fall 2017 archive; §§3.1 and 3.1.1 and the later discussion of the likelihood of voting paradoxes.
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the fixed archived entry were read through the page's extracted text; the entire entry was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §3.1 states the example's rankings and pairwise 2–1 cycle; §3.1.1 distinguishes Condorcet consistency from other voting methods and explains that some rules need a fallback when no Condorcet winner exists; the later likelihood discussion describes impartial-culture calculations and disagreement about empirical evidence and incomplete preference data.
sources.limitations: Archived secondary reference account, not the primary source. Its discussion surveys research rather than resolving the empirical debate; probability conclusions depend on stated preference-distribution assumptions.

sources.title: Arrow's Theorem
sources.author: Michael Morreau
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 13 October 2014, substantive revision 7 December 2025; §1, “The Will of the People?”
sources.access_level: Relevant passage in §1 and associated historical discussion were read through the page's extracted text; the entire entry was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §1 gives the three-person ABC/BCA/CAB majority cycle, calls it the paradox of voting, attributes its discovery to Condorcet (1785), distinguishes Condorcet's study of particular procedures from Arrow's axiomatic approach, and reports contrasting interpretations of Arrow's normative implications.
sources.limitations: Secondary interpretation. It establishes the conceptual and historical relationship but not that Arrow's theorem is logically derived from the three-option cycle. The article is not used as evidence that one normative reading is consensus.

sources.title: Complexities of Majority Voting
sources.author: Nicholas R. Miller
sources.publication: Vote Democracy project module for the Centre for Philosophy of Natural and Social Science, London School of Economics; revised April 2018 (original November 2015); §§4.2, 8.1, and sequential-voting discussion.
sources.access_level: Relevant passages of the PDF were read in the returned PDF text extraction; the full document was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: §4.2, text extraction's ‘Majority Voting’ pp. 10–11, describes three-option Condorcet cycles and cycles across more alternatives; §8.1, extracted pp. 39–40, explains sequential pairwise voting and how agenda order determines the final outcome when there is no Condorcet winner.
sources.limitations: A scholarly teaching module rather than a peer-reviewed journal article. Its agenda discussion concerns sequential pairwise procedures and should not be generalized to the pairwise-majority relation itself.

sources.title: Behavioural social choice: a status report
sources.author: Michel Regenwetter, Bernard Grofman, Anna Popova, William Messner, Clintin P. Davis-Stober, and Daniel R. Cavagnaro
sources.publication: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 364(1518), 833–843 (2009), especially §2, “The empirical rarity of the Condorcet paradox”; DOI 10.1098/rstb.2008.0259.
sources.access_level: Relevant full-text section (§2) was read in the PMC text extraction; the entire article was not read. Publisher metadata and abstract were separately consulted.
sources.exact_locations_read: §2 reviews impartial-culture model literature, reports the authors' critique that results can be sensitive to assumptions, and describes their account of survey and ballot evidence suggesting limited empirical support for cycles. The publisher page supplied publication date, author list, journal, volume, pages, and DOI.
sources.limitations: This is one scholarly position in a live debate, not a definitive prevalence estimate. Empirical detection depends on available preference data and the authors' interpretation of theoretical and observed evidence; Pacuit's reference account documents contrary views and data limitations.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The 1785 work is Condorcet's essay on majority decisions, and the original text discusses an election among three candidates with judgments about which candidate is preferable.
claim_evidence.source_title: Essai sur l'application de l'analyse à la probabilité des décisions rendues à la pluralité des voix; Social Choice Theory; Arrow's Theorem
claim_evidence.exact_location: Condorcet, Discours préliminaire, passage beginning “Il nous reste à donner un dernier exemple” and describing an election among three candidates; compare List §1.1 and Morreau §1 for bibliographic attribution and historical context.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary French OCR passage directly discusses three-candidate preference propositions and how majority judgments may yield inconsistent combinations. The secondary sources independently identify Condorcet's 1785 Essay with pairwise majority voting and the paradox.
claim_evidence.limitation: OCR is imperfect and only the relevant French excerpt was consulted. The original passage is not the exact modern profile table in the article; the displayed table is explicitly framed as an educational example.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: article identifies the original French passage and distinguishes it from the modern profile presentation.

claim_evidence.material_claim: For the displayed strict rankings A>B>C, B>C>A, and C>A>B, pairwise majority yields A>B, B>C, and C>A, each by 2–1.
claim_evidence.source_title: Revised article profile; Social Choice Theory; Voting Methods; Arrow's Theorem
claim_evidence.exact_location: Article §1, calculations directly derived from its table; Pacuit §3.1; List §1.1; Morreau §1, which report the equivalent three-person cycle under equivalent labels/ranking order.
claim_evidence.finding: Each pairwise count follows directly from the stated profile, and the three consulted reference accounts describe the same structural cycle. The table itself is a standard modern illustrative profile, not a verbatim primary-text quotation.
claim_evidence.limitation: The mathematical result is conditional on the stated rankings and one-vote-per-person pairwise majority rule; it is not a claim that every election cycles.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: displayed the rankings and explicitly stated the strict, transitive-ranking and pairwise-majority assumptions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The pairwise-majority relation can be intransitive even when every individual ranking is transitive; in this profile there is no Condorcet winner.
claim_evidence.source_title: Social Choice Theory; Voting Methods; Arrow's Theorem
claim_evidence.exact_location: List §1.1 defines the paradox and Condorcet winner; §3.1 defines pairwise majority and notes it does not guarantee transitive social preferences; Pacuit §3.1; Morreau §1.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources directly support the mathematical conclusion. The revised article says the pairwise relation exists but lacks a Condorcet winner, and does not infer that majority rule is universally incoherent.
claim_evidence.limitation: The conclusion is about this profile and rule; the result alone does not settle the normative status of majority rule.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the unqualified claim that majority will can be undefined with the narrower conclusion that no option beats every other under pairwise majority.

claim_evidence.material_claim: A cyclic pairwise relation and the outcome of sequential pairwise voting are distinct; agenda order can affect the final option under sequential procedure.
claim_evidence.source_title: Complexities of Majority Voting
claim_evidence.exact_location: Miller §4.2, pp. 10–11 in the text extraction, for the cycle; §8.1 and sequential pairwise voting discussion, pp. 39–40 in the text extraction, for procedure and agenda dependence.
claim_evidence.finding: Miller distinguishes the pairwise preference tournament from sequential committee procedure and explains why the order alternatives enter the sequential agenda can affect the winner when no Condorcet winner exists.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is conditional on a sequential procedure. The profile itself fixes each pairwise comparison; agenda dependence should not be attributed to the static relation alone.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified that order matters when pairwise votes are conducted sequentially, not when describing the cycle itself.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Condorcet-consistent methods elect a Condorcet winner when one exists, but a cycle leaves no such candidate and procedures need a fallback; a scoring method's selected outcome does not erase the pairwise cycle.
claim_evidence.source_title: Voting Methods
claim_evidence.exact_location: Pacuit §3.1.1, including the Condorcet rule and Copeland rule descriptions and discussion of scoring rules and Condorcet consistency.
claim_evidence.finding: The entry distinguishes a Condorcet-consistency criterion from other methods, shows that some rules need explicit treatment when no Condorcet winner exists, and explains that scoring rules need not select a Condorcet winner even when one exists.
claim_evidence.limitation: Different methods resolve or present cycles differently; no single fallback is implied by the paradox itself.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the blanket statement that scoring rules avoid cycles with the more precise distinction between selecting an outcome and making the pairwise relation transitive.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Single-peaked profiles prevent majority cycles under the stated domain restriction; this conditional result does not establish that actual electorates always meet the restriction.
claim_evidence.source_title: Social Choice Theory
claim_evidence.exact_location: List §3.3.1, ‘Relaxing universal domain,’ definition of single-peakedness and Black's result for odd electorates.
claim_evidence.finding: The reference states that single-peakedness ensures transitive majority preferences and a Condorcet winner at the median peak when the electorate is odd. The article retains this as a conditional mathematical result.
claim_evidence.limitation: Single-peakedness is a substantive restriction on admissible preferences, not a general property of elections.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly marked the result as conditional on the domain restriction.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Arrow's theorem is related to the Condorcet paradox but studies a broader class of aggregation procedures under axioms; the normative implications of impossibility results are disputed.
claim_evidence.source_title: Social Choice Theory; Arrow's Theorem
claim_evidence.exact_location: Morreau §1 distinguishes Condorcet's study of particular procedures from Arrow's general axiomatic approach and reports opposing interpretations; List §1.2 on Arrow's general framework and §3.1 on the basic aggregation framework.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources support treating Condorcet's paradox as a precursor and motivating illustration, while Arrow's theorem concerns broader conditions. They do not warrant saying Arrow's theorem is simply a consequence of this particular three-voter example.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article presents a concise historical relationship, not an exhaustive history of social-choice theory or a resolution of normative disputes.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the loose ‘motivated ... led to Arrow’s theorem’ claim with a qualified account of relation and distinction.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The probability of cycles depends on the assumed distribution of preferences; impartial culture is one model, while empirical prevalence and its interpretation remain disputed.
claim_evidence.source_title: Social Choice Theory; Voting Methods; Behavioural social choice: a status report
claim_evidence.exact_location: Pacuit's later discussion of the likelihood of voting paradoxes explains impartial-culture calculations, model assumptions and empirical-data limitations; List §3.1 describes sensitivity to preference-distribution departures; Regenwetter et al. §2 argues that theoretical predictions can be sensitive to assumptions and reports limited empirical support in studied data.
claim_evidence.finding: The sources agree that probability estimates are assumption-dependent but differ in their portrayal of the empirical risk. The article states that findings are disputed and that full pairwise-preference data are often unavailable; it does not assert a universal likelihood or consensus.
claim_evidence.limitation: Only relevant sections and one peer-reviewed article were examined, not the full empirical literature. Regenwetter et al.'s conclusions are one scholarly position; the reference account notes opposing interpretations and data-inference issues.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the frequency discussion by its preference-distribution assumptions and acknowledged empirical disagreement.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The fairness, legitimacy, and procedural evaluation questions are normative teaching prompts, not historical claims or conclusions proved by the cycle.
claim_evidence.source_title: Revised article framing; Arrow's Theorem
claim_evidence.exact_location: Article §§2, 4, and 6; Morreau §1 reports competing interpretations of the normative implications of Arrow's theorem.
claim_evidence.finding: The prompts are clearly labeled as questions. The revised exposition separates the mathematical finding from normative evaluation and avoids describing a contested interpretation as consensus.
claim_evidence.limitation: Editorial questions are not claims established by the cited sources.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: labeled fairness/legitimacy matters as normative discussion rather than mathematical conclusions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The dataset entry's date_verified and references match the revised article's Further Reading links in order.
claim_evidence.source_title: Matching Condorcet Paradox data record
claim_evidence.exact_location: Read-only data/experiments.json object with id condorcet-paradox and revised article §9, compared after the edit; reference order is the same and the patch sets date_verified to 2026-11-01.
claim_evidence.finding: All six proposed reference URLs match the revised article's Further Reading URLs exactly and in the same order. The patch has the matching id and date_verified 2026-11-01; the source descriptions distinguish a primary historical text from secondary reference and scholarly sources.
claim_evidence.limitation: Metadata reconciliation only; the dataset file remains unchanged and the patch is a local proposed patch, not applied data.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: created the local data-patch file; did not modify data/experiments.json.

unresolved_limits: The primary French essay was consulted only at the relevant passage in OCR text, not as a complete work or by inspection of the corresponding facsimile pages; the OCR may contain errors.
The article's three-voter table is an educational presentation of the standard cycle and is not claimed as a verbatim reproduction of Condorcet's exact original example.

The empirical frequency and practical significance of Condorcet cycles remain debated; this review read selected sources rather than an exhaustive literature review, and underlying elections often lack complete pairwise preference data.
Different voting rules handle cycles in different ways; the article names representative principles but does not survey all resolution methods or settle their merits.
No human subject-matter expert reviewed this entry.
